main_damage_causes: Reassignment of Sprout's most active and characterful line in the entire series – the exposure of Lockhart at the Chamber staff meeting – to Snape, removing her single greatest moment of agency and perceptive initiative

Omission of the Mandrake-lobbing sequence in the Battle of Hogwarts, which destroys the thematic payoff of her Herbology expertise as a weapon and reduces her to an undifferentiated background combatant

Loss of the Lockhart-at-the-greenhouse scene and the Venomous Tentacula beat, cumulatively stripping the texture that establishes her as a confident, unsentimental expert with professional pride who is being condescended to by a fraud

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 1 (Greenhouse Three, Mandrake lesson) – Lockhart intrusion
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that Sprout is 'looking distinctly disgruntled, not at all her usual cheerful self' when Lockhart closes the greenhouse door in her face after claiming to have shown her 'the right way to doctor a Whomping Willow.' She is visibly annoyed but the scene emphasises her authority is undermined by an interloper. Her competence and quiet resentment are both present.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film omits the Lockhart-at-the-greenhouse preamble entirely. Sprout simply appears in Greenhouse Three and begins the lesson without any scene of Lockhart upstaging her or closing the door in her face. The dynamic that establishes her as a professional being publicly condescended to by a fraud is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the Whomping Willow bandaging scene to show Sprout's competence being undermined by Lockhart while she maintains dignified irritation. Removing it means the film never establishes the contrast between her genuine expertise and his fraudulence in her own domain, flattening her characterisation as a skilled professional with professional pride.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 1 (Greenhouse Three) – Venomous Tentacula moment omitted
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 34-35: Sprout gives a sharp slap to the Venomous Tentacula as it inches sneakily over her shoulder, a small but vivid beat showing her hands-on confidence with dangerous plants and her unsentimental, no-nonsense physical authority in her own environment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Greenhouse Three lesson shows Sprout demonstrating Mandrake repotting competently but omits the Venomous Tentacula interaction. She simply instructs students and moves on.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but characteristic beat of Sprout's physical ease and fearlessness with dangerous plants is lost. It is a minor loss but contributes to the book's texture of her as instinctively at home in the greenhouse in a way the film does not replicate.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 3 (staff corridor scene / Chamber announcement) – Sprout's line reassigned to Snape
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 57: When the staff gather and McGonagall reveals a student has been taken, it is Professor Sprout who actively calls out Lockhart with 'That's right, Gilderoy. Weren't you saying just last night that you've known all along where the entrance to the Chamber of Secrets is?' This is a proactive, sharp, even gleeful exposure of Lockhart's fraud, showing Sprout as perceptive, assertive, and willing to act.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 (Scene 125): The equivalent challenge to Lockhart – 'Weren't you saying just last night that you've known all along where the entrance to the Chamber of Secrets is?' – is delivered by Snape, not Sprout. Sprout's only line in the scene is 'Who is it the monster's taken, Minerva?' She is reduced to a passive questioner.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most damaging single change to Sprout in the adaptation. The book gives her a moment of active agency: she is the one who exposes Lockhart and effectively forces his hand. It demonstrates her sharp intelligence, her awareness of Lockhart's fraud, and her willingness to act decisively when a child is in danger. Reassigning this to Snape – a character already well-established as antagonistic toward Lockhart – removes a defining moment of Sprout's character and transfers her agency to another. Snape doing it is expected; Sprout doing it is a revelation of character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH Part 2 Scene 5 (courtyard/castle defence) – McGonagall delivers Sprout's line
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 189: When Flitwick warns that nothing they do will keep Voldemort out indefinitely, it is Professor Sprout who replies 'But we can hold him up.' McGonagall then thanks her warmly ('Thank you, Pomona') and between the two witches 'there passed a look of grim understanding.' Sprout then immediately takes charge, hurrying toward the door saying 'I shall meet you in the Great Hall in twenty minutes with my House,' and is heard muttering about Tentacula, Devil's Snare and Snargaluff pods as she jogs away.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film DH2 Scene 5: Flitwick delivers his caveat about not being able to keep Voldemort out indefinitely. In the film it is Madam Sprout (listed as such in the script) who says 'That doesn't mean we can hold him up' – but the line is immediately repeated verbatim by McGonagall, and the warmth of 'Thank you, Pomona' with the look of grim understanding between the two witches is absent. The muttered aside about Tentacula, Devil's Snare and Snargaluff pods as she jogs away – one of her most characterful moments in the entire saga – is also omitted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version gives Sprout a moment of quiet determination that earns an explicit acknowledgement from McGonagall and a relationship beat between two senior witches. Her muttered gardening-as-weaponry aside is uniquely characteristic – it shows her mind immediately going to practical, botanical solutions even in crisis. The film has the line but strips the acknowledgement, the relationship dynamic, and the follow-through monologue, significantly diluting the scene's contribution to her characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH Part 2 Scene 7 (courtyard battle) – Sprout as background combatant only
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 197-198: Sprout is shown thundering past Harry followed by Neville and others, all wearing earmuffs and carrying large potted plants – Mandrakes – to be lobbed over the walls. She is actively leading a tactical deployment of her botanical expertise as a weapon, a direct callback to her Herbology teaching across the series.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film DH2 Scene 7: Sprout appears in the courtyard battle scene trading spells with Death Eaters alongside others. The Mandrake-lobbing sequence that is her signature contribution to the battle – the moment where her specific expertise as Herbology professor becomes directly militarily useful – is not depicted. She is simply one combatant among many.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Mandrake deployment is narratively important because it completes a thematic arc: the plants she taught students to handle safely in Book/Film 2 become weapons in the final battle. It is also the clearest expression of Sprout's particular contribution to the defence of Hogwarts. Without it, she is an interchangeable background combatant rather than a character whose specific role in the saga has been building to this moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 3 (Dumbledore's announcement) – Sprout named but not present as agent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 53: McGonagall announces 'Professor Sprout has informed me that the Mandrakes are ready for cutting at last. Tonight, we will be able to revive those who have been Petrified.' Sprout's care of the Mandrakes across the year is thus directly credited as the solution to the central crisis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film CoS Scene 3 (Scene 137, end feast): Dumbledore credits 'Professor Sprout and Madam Pomfrey, whose Mandrake Juice has been successfully administered.' This is faithful in crediting her. No damage here.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is largely faithful – Sprout is credited. The framing is slightly less active (Dumbledore announces it as a fait accompli rather than McGonagall announcing her work in progress) but this is a very minor shift and does not constitute meaningful damage. Scored minimally for the record.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film HBP Scene 4 (greenhouse/vegetable patch) – Sprout reduced to a prop
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 150-154: Sprout is present at the vegetable patch in conversation with Slughorn, speaking warmly and collegially ('Oh, I quite agree. That enough for you?'), then heading off into the gathering darkness toward her greenhouses. She is characterised as a knowledgeable peer of Slughorn, sharing expertise on the timing of plant harvesting.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film HBP Scene 4: The scene is restructured so that Harry observes Slughorn through the greenhouse panes and then encounters him outside. Sprout is referenced only in Harry's joke – 'You probably feared I was Madam Sprout' – and Slughorn confirms this ('Well, yes, actually'). Sprout herself does not appear. She exists only as a threat Slughorn is hiding from, not as an active participant.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene gives Sprout a brief but warm, collegial moment that shows her professional relationship with other staff. The film replaces her physical presence with a reference to her as someone to be avoided, which is mildly reductive. The damage is minor given the brevity of the original scene.
